section.title: The Bronze Serpent
section.sectionRationale: This chapter turns the corner from forty years of wandering to the first real victories on the way into the land, but at its heart sits one of the Old Testament's most explicitly Christ-shaped scenes: a dying people healed by looking, in faith, at the very image of the judgment God sent against them. Jesus Himself later takes this scene as His own explanation of the cross.
section.thesis: When Israel's impatience turns to open sin against God, He sends venomous snakes among them, yet in the same breath provides healing through a bronze serpent lifted up on a pole, so that anyone who simply looks at it in faith lives, a scene Jesus later applies directly to His own being lifted up on the cross.
section.frameNote: Four movements: victory over Arad and the vow at Hormah; the people's impatience, the snakes, and the bronze serpent lifted up for healing; the journey and the well-song through Moabite territory; and the defeat of Sihon and Og, opening the way east of the Jordan.

verses.text: When the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev, heard that Israel was coming along the road to Atharim, he attacked Israel and captured some prisoners.
So Israel made a vow to the LORD: “If You will deliver this people into our hands, we will devote their cities to destruction.”
And the LORD heard Israel's plea and delivered up the Canaanites. Israel devoted them and their cities to destruction; so they named the place Hormah.

units.label: Impatience, snakes, and the bronze serpent

media.alt: A bronze serpent lifted up on a pole against the desert sky
media.caption: Whoever is bitten and looks at the bronze serpent will live.

verses.text: Then they set out from Mount Hor along the route to the Red Sea, in order to bypass the land of Edom. But the people grew impatient on the journey
and spoke against God and against Moses: “Why have you led us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread or water, and we detest this wretched food!”
So the LORD sent {{venomous|venomous}} snakes among the people, and many of the Israelites were bitten and died.

Then the people came to Moses and said, “We have sinned by speaking against the LORD and against you. Intercede with the LORD so He will take the snakes away from us.” So Moses interceded for the people.
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live.”
So Moses made a {{bronzeserpent|bronze snake}} and mounted it on a pole. If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live.
Then the Israelites set out and camped at Oboth.
They journeyed from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim in the wilderness opposite Moab to the east.
From there they set out and camped in the Valley of Zered.
From there they moved on and camped on the other side of the Arnon, in the wilderness that extends into the Amorite territory. Now the Arnon is the border between the Moabites and the Amorites.
Therefore it is stated in the Book of the Wars of the LORD: “Waheb in Suphah and the wadis of the Arnon,
even the slopes of the wadis that extend to the site of Ar and lie along the border of Moab.”
From there they went on to Beer, the well where the LORD said to Moses, “Gather the people so that I may give them water.”
Then Israel sang this song: “Spring up, O well, all of you sing to it!
The princes dug the well; the nobles of the people hollowed it out with their scepters and with their staffs.” From the wilderness the Israelites went on to Mattanah,
and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth,
and from Bamoth to the valley in Moab where the top of Pisgah overlooks the wasteland.

units.label: Sihon and Og defeated
units.note: the land east of the Jordan taken

verses.text: Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying,
“Let us pass through your land. We will not cut through any field or vineyard, or drink water from any well. We will stay on the King's Highway until we have passed through your territory.”
But Sihon would not let Israel pass through his territory. Instead, he gathered his whole army and went out to confront Israel in the wilderness. When he came to Jahaz, he fought against Israel.
And Israel put him to the sword and took possession of his land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, but only up to the border of the Ammonites, because it was fortified.
Israel captured all the cities of the Amorites and occupied them, including Heshbon and all its villages.
Heshbon was the city of Sihon king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land as far as the Arnon.
That is why the poets say: “Come to Heshbon, let it be rebuilt; let the city of Sihon be restored.
For a fire went out from Heshbon, a blaze from the city of Sihon. It consumed Ar of Moab, the rulers of Arnon's heights.
Woe to you, O Moab! You are destroyed, O people of Chemosh! He gave up his sons as refugees, and his daughters into captivity to Sihon king of the Amorites.
But we have overthrown them; Heshbon is destroyed as far as Dibon. We demolished them as far as Nophah, which reaches to Medeba.”
So Israel lived in the land of the Amorites.
After Moses had sent spies to Jazer, Israel captured its villages and drove out the Amorites who were there.
Then they turned and went up the road to Bashan, and Og king of Bashan and his whole army came out to meet them in battle at Edrei.

But the LORD said to Moses, “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land. Do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon.”
So they struck down Og, along with his sons and his whole army, until no remnant was left. And they took possession of his land.

venomous.gloss: Fiery or burning serpent, describing the sharp burning pain of the venom. The same root, saraph, later names the seraphim, burning ones, though here it describes the deadly bite God sent as judgment for Israel's contempt of His provision.

bronzeserpent.gloss: Made of bronze, nechoshet, the same word later used for the object's proper name, Nehushtan, in 2 Kings 18:4. The bronze serpent was not magical but a God-appointed sign: healing came not from the object but from looking to it in obedient faith.

basic.context: After forty years, Israel finally begins to make real progress toward the land, winning battles at Hormah and later against Sihon and Og. But in the middle of this progress, the people's old pattern of impatient complaint returns, and God sends venomous snakes as judgment. When the people repent, God provides an unusual remedy: a bronze snake on a pole that anyone bitten could look at and live.
basic.hermeneutics: This really happened to a real, dying people in the wilderness, and it is not primarily a story about snakes but about faith: healing came only to those who trusted God enough to look at the very thing shaped like their affliction. Jesus later reads this event as directly about Himself, so the passage carries genuine typological weight, not merely moral lessons.
basic.originalLanguages: The snakes are called nachash saraph, fiery serpents, a burning venom that matches the burning complaint that provoked God's judgment. The remedy God commands is a nechoshet, bronze, image of that very serpent, later called Nehushtan, so that Israel's healing came by looking, in faith, at the image of their own judgment lifted up before them.
basic.typology: Jesus Himself draws the line in John 3:14-15: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life. The serpent, symbol of the judgment against sin, is lifted up so the dying can look and live, exactly as Christ, bearing the judgment for sin though sinless Himself, is lifted up on the cross so that all who look to Him in faith are saved.
basic.christ: This is one of the most direct pieces of Old Testament typology in all of Scripture, because Jesus names it Himself. He compares His own crucifixion to this bronze serpent: lifted up publicly, bearing the very form of the judgment against sin, so that everyone who simply looks to Him in faith, rather than earning healing by effort, receives eternal life.
basic.god: God is just, sending real judgment on real rebellion, yet He is also astonishingly gracious, providing a way of healing before the people even finish asking, and making that healing available to anyone who will simply look in faith. His holiness and His mercy meet in the very object of judgment becoming the means of life.
basic.crossReferences: John 3:14-15 is Jesus' own direct application of this scene to His crucifixion. 2 Kings 18:4 records that centuries later King Hezekiah destroyed this same bronze serpent because Israel had begun to worship it, a warning against turning a gift of grace into an idol. 1 Corinthians 10:9 warns against testing Christ as some of the Israelites did in the wilderness.
basic.oneStory: A people under judgment, dying from the very poison of their own rebellion, are healed not by their own effort but by simply looking, in faith, at the sign God provided. That pattern of faith rather than works, looking rather than achieving, runs straight through Scripture to the cross, where Jesus Himself said He would be lifted up exactly as this serpent was, so that everyone who looks to Him in faith might live forever.

context.literary:
Numbers 21 is a hinge chapter, and its shape tells the reader so. It opens at Arad in the far south, verse 1, and closes with Og's land in Bashan in the far north, verse 35. In between, Israel travels the whole length of the land east of the Jordan. The first scene deliberately rewrites an old defeat. In Numbers 14:45 the Amalekites and Canaanites routed Israel 'all the way to Hormah' when the people went up without the LORD. Now the place of that humiliation becomes the place of victory, and the name Hormah, 'destruction,' is given a new meaning, verse 3. The new generation succeeds where the old one failed, because this time they ask the LORD first, verse 2.

The bronze serpent scene, verses 4 to 9, is a tight miniature of every wilderness rebellion: complaint, judgment, confession, intercession, remedy. What is new is the remedy. Earlier judgments simply stopped when Moses prayed or Aaron made atonement, Numbers 11:2 and 16:47-48. Here the snakes stay, and God gives a sign to look at in the middle of the danger.

The rest of the chapter changes texture. The narrative becomes an itinerary, verses 10 to 20, broken by three pieces of poetry: a fragment from the Book of the Wars of the LORD, verses 14 and 15, the song of the well, verses 17 and 18, and the taunt song over Heshbon, verses 27 to 30. The poems slow the reader down at the points where God's provision and victory are being celebrated. The first war poem names geography; the well song names water given without striking a rock; the Heshbon song names a conquest.

The closing battles are told in parallel. Israel asks Sihon for passage in the very words it had used with Edom, verse 22 and Numbers 20:17. Edom's refusal ended with Israel turning away; Sihon's refusal ends with his kingdom in Israel's hands. Og's defeat is then narrated as a repeat of Sihon's, 'Do to him as you did to Sihon,' verse 34, which sets up the pattern of conquest Joshua will follow.
context.historical:
The chapter belongs to the fortieth year after the exodus. Aaron has just died on Mount Hor, Numbers 20:28, which Numbers 33:38 dates to the fifth month of that year. Moses later marks the crossing of the Zered, verse 12, as the end of the thirty eight years of wandering, 'until that entire generation of fighting men had perished,' Deuteronomy 2:13-14. The people who complain in verse 5 are therefore largely the children of the exodus generation, speaking their parents' words.

The route matters. Edom had refused passage, Numbers 20:14-21, so Israel turned south from Mount Hor toward the Gulf of Aqaba and then swung north around Edom and Moab through the arid country east of them. Numbers 33:41-44 lists the stations, including Zalmonah and Punon. Punon is usually identified with the copper district of Feinan in the Arabah, and the Arabah held other ancient copper mines, among them Timna, where excavators found a small copper snake in a shrine used in the period of Midianite presence there. That does not explain the bronze serpent, but it shows that snakes and copper working belonged to the landscape Israel was crossing. The region still has venomous snakes, as Deuteronomy 8:15 remembers.

The King's Highway of verse 22 was the main north to south road on the plateau east of the Jordan. Sihon's kingdom lay between the Arnon and the Jabbok, with Heshbon as its capital, and verse 26 records that Sihon had himself taken this land from Moab. That detail matters later, when Jephthah answers an Ammonite claim by retelling this chapter, Judges 11:19-26. Several places named here, Dibon, Medeba, Jahaz and the Arnon, appear on the Moabite Stone of King Mesha from the ninth century BC, which also names Chemosh, 'the god of Moab.' Og of Bashan is remembered as one of the last of the Rephaim, whose iron bed was still shown in Rabbah, Deuteronomy 3:11. To the first hearers, the defeat of these two kings was the first installment of the land promise.
context.canonical:
The victories over Sihon and Og became one of Israel's standard confessions of God's power. Moses rehearses them at length, Deuteronomy 2:24 to 3:11, and the Levites include them in their great prayer, Nehemiah 9:22. Rahab in Jericho has already heard the news, Joshua 2:10, as have the Gibeonites, Joshua 9:10. Psalm 135:10-12 and Psalm 136:17-22 sing of 'Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan' by name, and Amos 2:9 recalls the Amorite whose height was like the cedars.

The Heshbon taunt song of verses 27 to 30 has its own afterlife. Jeremiah borrows it for his oracle against Moab: 'fire has gone forth from Heshbon and a flame from within Sihon,' Jeremiah 48:45, followed by 'Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished,' verse 46, very close to Numbers 21:29.

The serpent's own story runs in two directions. Kept in Israel for centuries, it became an object of worship, and Hezekiah 'demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it,' 2 Kings 18:4. The same object that once pointed to God's word had become a rival to it. Psalm 107:17-20 preserves the pattern of the episode without naming it: rebels suffer, cry out, and God 'sent forth His word and healed them.' A Jewish writing from the period between the Testaments, the Wisdom of Solomon, already insisted that the one who turned toward the sign was saved not by the thing he saw but by God, the Saviour of all.

The New Testament takes up the scene twice. Paul warns the Corinthians not to test Christ 'as some of them did, and were killed by snakes,' 1 Corinthians 10:9, and says these things were written 'as warnings for us,' verse 11. Jesus Himself makes it the key to His death: 'Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,' John 3:14, a thread John picks up again in John 8:28 and 12:32-33.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote this chapter for a people about to cross the Jordan, and he wanted them to see two things side by side. The first is that the old disease had not died with the old generation. The children of the exodus, at the very edge of success, repeat the words of their parents almost exactly: 'Why have you led us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?' verse 5, compare Numbers 14:2-3 and 20:4-5. Victory at Hormah did not make them immune to contempt for God's daily gift.

The second is that the LORD's answer to this generation is different in texture. When they confess, He does not simply remove the danger; He appoints a way to live through it that depends entirely on taking Him at His word. Israel was meant to learn that its life in the land would be the same: surrounded by threats it could not remove, it would live by trusting and obeying what God had said.

The framing victories carry the rest of the message. The LORD who heals the bitten is the LORD who delivers kings. The same God who promised life to all who looked says 'Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand,' verse 34. The first hearers were to go into Canaan remembering both.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything here is narrative, and it should be read that way. The vow of verse 2 and the destruction of Arad's cities belong to the particular command of cherem given for the conquest, and they are not a pattern for how believers treat enemies now, since Jesus tells His people to 'love your enemies,' Matthew 5:44. Nor does the bronze serpent license images for healing or devotion. The later worship of Nehushtan, 2 Kings 18:4, shows how quickly a God-given sign can be turned into a charm, and Hezekiah is praised for destroying it.

What does carry forward is taught explicitly by the New Testament. Paul reads the complaint and the snakes as a warning against testing Christ and grumbling, 1 Corinthians 10:9-11. Jesus reads the lifted serpent as the shape of the gospel, John 3:14-15. The instruction for today is therefore not 'make a pole' but 'look to the Son and believe,' which is how John 6:40 puts it.

debates.question: Why did healing come through looking at an image of the very thing that was killing them?

views.label: A sign that pictured the curse overcome
views.case: The serpent on the pole was the judgment itself held up, fixed and harmless. To look at it was to see the thing that bit you already mastered by God's word. This reading takes seriously that God told Moses to make a saraph, the same word as the snakes, verse 8, so that the remedy mirrored the wound.

views.label: A test of trust in God's word alone
views.case: The object had no power in itself, which is why it could later be destroyed without loss, 2 Kings 18:4. What saved was believing the promise attached to it, 'he will live,' verse 8. The Wisdom of Solomon already read it this way in Judaism before Christ.

views.label: A deliberate reversal of pagan snake charms
views.case: Snake images were used across the ancient world as protective charms. On this reading God takes a familiar symbol and strips it of magic by attaching it to a spoken command, so that healing plainly comes from Him and not from the bronze.

debates.bearing: The views work together more than they compete. The shape of the sign mattered, because Jesus draws on it when He speaks of being lifted up in the likeness of what condemns us, Romans 8:3. But the power lay entirely in God's promise, received by looking. The later idolatry shows what happens when the sign is kept and the promise is forgotten.

debates.question: Does Jesus in John 3:14 compare Himself to the serpent, or to the act of lifting up?

views.label: The point is the lifting up and the looking
views.case: Jesus' sentence is built on the verbs: Moses lifted up, the Son of Man must be lifted up, everyone who believes may have life. On this view Jesus is not identifying with a snake at all, a creature associated with the enemy since Genesis 3, but with the public exposure and the promise of life to all who look.

views.label: The serpent itself pictures Christ made sin
views.case: The object lifted up bore the form of the judgment, and Paul says God made Christ 'to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, sending Him 'in the likeness of sinful man,' Romans 8:3. Many interpreters from the church fathers onward have seen in the bronze serpent a picture of the sinless One bearing the likeness of the curse, Galatians 3:13.

debates.bearing: John's wording keeps the stress on the lifting up and the believing, and the reader should not press the snake into a portrait of Jesus' person. Yet the object was chosen because it resembled the curse, and the New Testament does say Christ bore the curse. Both elements belong to the comparison, with the emphasis where Jesus puts it.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 4 says the people 'grew impatient,' literally that the soul of the people became short, qatsar nephesh. The same idiom describes Samson worn down by Delilah until 'he was sick to death,' Judges 16:16. Strikingly, it is also used of God Himself in Judges 10:16, where 'He could no longer bear the misery of Israel.' The phrase describes a patience that has run out. Israel's patience with God runs out here; in Judges God's patience runs out, not with Israel's sin but with Israel's suffering.

The 'wretched food' of verse 5 is described with an adjective built from the root qalal, to be light, slight or contemptible. It is the same root Genesis 12:3 uses for 'those who curse you,' the ones who treat Abraham's family as of no account. The manna was God's daily gift, called 'grain from heaven' in Psalm 78:24, and Israel calls it contemptible. The complaint itself contains a contradiction: 'There is no bread,' and in the same breath, 'we detest this wretched food.'

The snakes are saraphim, from saraph, a root meaning to burn. The same noun appears in Deuteronomy 8:15, and in Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6 Isaiah speaks of a saraph that flies, the 'flying serpent.' The plural is the word for the seraphim who stand above the LORD in Isaiah 6:2, the burning ones of His holiness. In verse 8 God tells Moses to make simply 'a saraph,' a burning one. Moses makes a nechash nechoshet, a snake of bronze, and the two words sound almost alike, so that the remedy echoes the wound even in its name.

The 'pole' of verse 8 is nes, a word usually meaning a banner, standard or signal raised for people to see and rally to. Moses named an altar 'The LORD Is My Banner,' Exodus 17:15, using the same word, and Isaiah pictures the Root of Jesse standing 'as a banner for the peoples,' Isaiah 11:10, to which the nations will come, compare Isaiah 49:22. The Greek translation of Numbers renders it 'sign.' The bronze serpent was not merely held up; it was raised as a rallying point.

Two verbs for looking appear. In verse 8 God says anyone who 'looks at it' will live, using the ordinary verb for seeing, ra'ah. In verse 9 the narrator uses hibbit, a stronger verb for turning one's gaze toward something. It is the verb of Zechariah 12:10, 'they will look on Me, the One they have pierced,' which John 19:37 applies to the crucifixion, and of Isaiah 51:1, 'Look to the rock from which you were cut.' It is a deliberate, directed look.

When Jesus takes up the scene, John uses hypsoo, 'lift up,' John 3:14. The verb can mean physical raising and also exaltation. The Greek translation of Isaiah 52:13 uses it of the Servant who will be 'lifted up and highly exalted.' John exploits both senses: the cross is at once the lifting of a condemned man on a pole and the exaltation of the Son. John 12:33 makes the physical sense explicit: 'He said this to indicate the kind of death He was going to die.'

Finally, the vow of verse 2 uses the root charam, to devote to destruction, as the BSB footnote explains, and 'Hormah' comes from the same root. The place name that once marked Israel's defeat, Numbers 14:45, now marks the fulfilled vow.

typology.type: The bronze serpent lifted up on a pole
typology.fulfillment: The type is declared by Jesus, not discovered by interpreters: 'Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,' John 3:14. The correspondence is in the lifting, in the public exposure, and in life given to all who look. The escalation is great. The serpent healed bodies that would still die; the Son gives 'eternal life,' John 3:15, and 'shall not perish,' John 3:16. Where the type falls short is that bronze could only point; it bore nothing. Christ does not merely display the curse but bears it, Galatians 3:13, and His lifting is also His exaltation, John 12:32.

typology.type: Looking as the whole of the response
typology.fulfillment: The bitten Israelite did nothing but turn his eyes to what God had raised. That pattern runs into the gospel, where Jesus says the Father's will is that 'everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life,' John 6:40, and Hebrews calls believers to 'fix our eyes on Jesus,' Hebrews 12:2. Isaiah 45:22 extends the call to all nations: 'Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.' The type falls short in that one look healed one bite; faith in Christ is a looking that continues, a whole life turned toward Him.

typology.type: Moses interceding for a guilty people
typology.fulfillment: The people ask Moses to pray, and 'Moses interceded for the people,' verse 7, as he had in Exodus 32:30-32 and as Psalm 106:23 remembers, standing 'in the breach.' The pattern reaches its fullness in Christ, the 'one mediator between God and men,' 1 Timothy 2:5, who 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near through Him, Hebrews 7:25. Moses could pray and receive a remedy; Christ is Himself both the one who intercedes and the remedy lifted up. Moses' intercession ended with his death outside the land; Christ's never ends.

typology.type: Water given at Beer, the well
typology.fulfillment: After the snakes, God gathers the people and says 'I may give them water,' verse 16, and they sing to a well dug with staffs, not struck from a rock in anger as at Meribah, Numbers 20:11-12. Paul says the rock that followed Israel was Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4, and Jesus offers water that becomes 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14, compare John 7:37-38. This is a gentler echo than the serpent, a theme more than a declared type, and it falls short in that a well must be dug and can run dry, while the Spirit Christ gives flows from within.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by His own word. John 3:14-15 comes in the middle of Jesus' conversation with Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel who knew this chapter well. Jesus uses it to explain the new birth He has just described. Nicodemus asked, 'How can this be?' John 3:9, and Jesus answers by pointing to a scene every Israelite knew: dying people who were saved by looking at what God had raised up. The verse that follows is the most quoted sentence in the Bible, 'For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son,' John 3:16. The love of John 3:16 is explained by the lifted serpent of John 3:14. God's love is not described in the abstract; it takes the shape of the pole in the wilderness.

The word 'must' in John 3:14 matters. The lifting up is not an accident that befell Jesus; it is necessary, as necessary as the pole was to the bitten Israelites. John returns to it twice. 'When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am He,' John 8:28. The cross will reveal who Jesus is. And 'when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw everyone to Myself,' John 12:32, which John explains as a reference to 'the kind of death He was going to die,' verse 33. The nes of Numbers 21:8 was a banner to rally to; the lifted Christ draws people from every nation.

The chapter leads to Christ by the shape of the remedy. The thing lifted up resembled the curse. Paul says that God sent 'His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin,' and in that flesh 'condemned sin,' Romans 8:3. He says that God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that Christ became 'a curse for us,' since the law pronounced a curse on 'everyone who is hung on a tree,' Galatians 3:13. On the pole the serpent was harmless, the curse held up and mastered. On the cross the curse is not merely displayed but exhausted.

It leads to Christ by the kind of response it calls for. The Israelite contributed nothing to his healing. He could not neutralise the venom or earn the cure; he could only turn and look. Peter joins the healing and the cross in a single sentence: 'He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree,' and 'By His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24, quoting Isaiah 53:5. John records that the soldiers who pierced Jesus fulfilled the word, 'They will look on the One they have pierced,' John 19:37.

The rest of the chapter contributes too, though more quietly. The complaint about manna, 'this wretched food,' is answered in John 6, where Jesus calls Himself 'the bread of life,' John 6:35, the true bread from heaven that the manna pictured. And the victories over Sihon and Og, given before Israel crossed the Jordan, anticipate the Christ who 'must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet,' 1 Corinthians 15:25.

Caution keeps the reading honest. The snake does not become a portrait of Jesus' character, and the details of the pole or the metal are not coded messages. What the New Testament draws out is the lifting up, the likeness to the curse, and life for all who look. Those three are enough, and they are enough to make this one of the clearest gospel pictures in the Torah.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who takes words seriously. The people's sin in verse 5 is speech: they 'spoke against God and against Moses.' The judgment matches the offence. Venom enters through the mouth of a snake as contempt had come out of the mouth of the people. Yet the healing also comes through speech, God's own word in verse 8, 'he will live.' The chapter is framed by the power of what is said, and it vindicates God's word over Israel's.

He is a God who answers prayer. The chapter opens with Israel's vow and the notice that 'the LORD heard Israel's plea,' verse 3. It turns on Moses' intercession, verse 7. It closes with God speaking unasked to reassure Moses before Og, verse 34. The LORD is not distant from His people's needs, whether the need is victory, healing or courage.

His judgment is real and personal. Scripture does not say the snakes happened to be in the area; 'the LORD sent venomous snakes,' verse 6. The covenant had warned of this very thing, 'I will send wild animals against you,' Leviticus 26:22, and the prophets later use the same language, 'I will send snakes among you,' Jeremiah 8:17. The God who gives manna can also withdraw protection, and He does so because contempt for His gifts is contempt for Him.

His mercy does not work by pretending the danger is gone. The people ask Him to 'take the snakes away,' verse 7. He does not. Instead He provides a way to live while the snakes remain. That is a profound picture of grace in a fallen world. God does not always remove the consequences of sin at once, but He never leaves His people without a remedy. It is the same God who told Israel at Marah, 'I am the LORD who heals you,' Exodus 15:26.

He is also jealous for His own glory, even against His own gifts. The bronze serpent was His command, and centuries later its destruction was counted as faithfulness, 2 Kings 18:4. God will not share His worship with the instruments of His grace. What He gives is meant to point to Him.

The chapter holds together God's sovereignty over nations and His care for a single bitten person. The same LORD who delivers Sihon and Og, whose defeat Psalm 136:17-22 sings of with the refrain 'His loving devotion endures forever,' is the LORD who promises life to 'anyone who is bitten,' verse 8. His purposes are as large as the conquest of kingdoms and as small as one dying man's glance.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to turn our eyes rather than our efforts. The right answer to God's judgment is not self-rescue but confession and trust in the remedy He has raised. And it teaches thankfulness for daily grace, since the sin that began the whole scene was calling God's daily bread 'wretched.'

crossReferences.note: The earlier rout 'all the way to Hormah,' when the first generation went up without the ark or Moses. Numbers 21:1-3 reverses it at the same place. The difference is that the new generation asks the LORD before fighting, and the name of defeat becomes the name of a fulfilled vow.

Moses dates the crossing of the Zered, Numbers 21:12, as the end of thirty eight years of wandering, when the whole generation of fighting men had died. The complaint of Numbers 21:5 comes from their children, showing how deeply the old pattern had been learned.

Moses recalls the 'vast and terrifying wilderness with its venomous snakes and scorpions' and the water brought from the rock. The same Hebrew phrase for the snakes appears, and Moses remembers them not as a curse but as part of the LORD's leading, meant to humble Israel and teach dependence.

Hezekiah demolishes 'the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made' because Israel had burned incense to it. The sign given for healing had become an idol. The account is a lasting warning that God's instruments of grace must never replace God Himself.

Rebels suffer affliction, draw 'near to the gates of death,' cry out, and God 'sent forth His word and healed them.' The psalm gathers the shape of Numbers 21:4-9 into a pattern of praise: healing comes by the word of the LORD in answer to the cry of the guilty.

Jesus Himself applies the scene to His death: 'so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.' The looking of Numbers 21:9 becomes believing, and physical life becomes eternal life, in the verses that lead straight into John 3:16.

Jesus says that when He is lifted up from the earth He will draw everyone to Himself, and John explains that this indicated 'the kind of death He was going to die.' The lifted serpent was a rallying banner, nes, for the dying; the crucified Christ draws people from every nation.

Paul names this episode directly, 'We should not test Christ, as some of them did, and were killed by snakes,' and says it was written as a warning for those on whom the fulfilment of the ages has come. The complaint of Numbers 21:5 is treated as a live danger for the church.

Christ redeemed us from the curse by 'becoming a curse for us,' since 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.' The bronze serpent on its pole bore the likeness of the judgment; Christ on the tree bore the curse itself, which is why looking to Him brings life.

The LORD promises that His people 'will look on Me, the One they have pierced,' using the same verb of turning one's gaze that Numbers 21:9 uses. John 19:37 applies it to the crucifixion. Looking in grief and looking in faith converge at the cross.

The people of Numbers 21:5 despised the manna as 'wretched food.' Jesus, reflecting on the manna in John 6:31-34, says 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger.' The gift Israel scorned pointed to the Son who is Himself God's daily bread.

The psalm names 'Sihon king of the Amorites' and 'Og king of Bashan' with the refrain 'His loving devotion endures forever' after each line. The battles of Numbers 21:21-35 become an act of worship, remembered as expressions of covenant love rather than mere military success.

Jeremiah reuses the Heshbon taunt song of Numbers 21:28-29 for his own oracle against Moab: fire from Heshbon, a flame from Sihon, and 'Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished.' The old victory song becomes prophecy of Moab's later fall.

Jephthah answers an Ammonite claim to the land by retelling Numbers 21:21-24 almost word for word: the request to pass, Sihon's refusal, the battle at Jahaz, and the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok. The chapter served as Israel's title deed east of the Jordan.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 set a serpent at the start of humanity's trouble. The serpent spoke against God's word, and the man and woman listened. Death entered through that conversation. Numbers 21 is not a retelling of Genesis 3, but it lives in its shadow. Once again people speak against God, once again serpents bring death, and once again the question is whether God's word or the word of distrust will be believed.

The chapter also answers the long story of Numbers. The first generation died in the wilderness because they 'refused to believe' God, Numbers 14:11, and Hebrews 3:19 concludes 'it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter.' Their children now stand at the threshold, and the same unbelief flares up. What is different is that God provides a way for faith to live in the very place where unbelief brought death. Healing comes by believing the promise, which is exactly what the first generation would not do.

The story moves forward from here into conquest. The defeat of Sihon and Og is the first taste of the promise to Abraham that his offspring would possess the land, and it gives Israel a pattern to remember when facing Jericho. But the bronze serpent itself travels a stranger road. Preserved in Israel, it became Nehushtan, an idol, and had to be broken, 2 Kings 18:4. Israel's history shows again and again that even God's gifts could not cure the heart that kept turning away.

The story comes to rest in Christ. Jesus takes the lifted serpent as the explanation of His cross, John 3:14-15. Here the old enemy of Genesis 3 is answered at last. The seed of the woman, whose heel the serpent strikes, is lifted up on a tree, bearing the curse, and by that death He destroys 'him who holds the power of death,' Hebrews 2:14. The serpent's head is crushed in the very act that looks like the serpent's victory. Paul can promise the church that 'the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet,' Romans 16:20.

The new creation completes the picture. 'That ancient serpent called the devil and Satan' is hurled down, Revelation 12:9, and later seized and bound, Revelation 20:2. The river of the water of life flows from the throne, and the leaves of the tree of life 'are for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:1-2. The people who once looked at a bronze image on a pole in a waterless land will look on the face of the Lamb in a city with a river, and the healing that began with a glance will be complete and permanent.

sermon.title: Moses and the Bronze Serpent
sermon.why: Preached on Numbers 21:4-9 and John 3:12-17, Keller draws out exactly how the bronze serpent lifted up for a dying people foreshadows Christ lifted up on the cross, and what it means to look to Him in simple faith rather than earn healing by effort.

quiz.q: What provoked the LORD to send venomous snakes among the people in this chapter?

options.text: The people grew impatient and spoke against God and Moses, detesting the food He provided.
options.note: Verses 4 to 5 record this complaint directly before the snakes appear.

options.text: Israel's defeat in battle against the king of Arad.
options.note: That battle actually ended in Israel's victory at Hormah, not defeat, and is unrelated to the snakes.

options.text: Aaron's death on Mount Hor in the previous chapter.
options.note: Aaron's death is recorded earlier, but the snakes are tied specifically to this chapter's complaint against God's provision.

options.text: No reason is given for the snakes.
options.note: Verses 4 to 6 clearly connect the snakes to the people's complaint.

quiz.q: What did God instruct Moses to make so that the bitten people could be healed?

options.text: A bronze serpent mounted on a pole, to be looked at by anyone bitten.
options.note: Verses 8 to 9 describe this exact instruction and its fulfillment.

options.text: A special herbal remedy applied to the snakebites.
options.note: No remedy of this kind appears; the healing came through looking at the bronze serpent.

options.text: A tent set apart where the bitten could be quarantined.
options.note: The text describes no quarantine, only the command to look at the bronze serpent.

options.text: Nothing; the plague simply ran its course.
options.note: Verses 8 to 9 record a specific, God-given remedy.

quiz.q: How does Jesus Himself apply this bronze serpent scene, according to John 3:14-15?

options.text: He compares His own being lifted up on the cross to the serpent being lifted up, so that believers may have eternal life.
options.note: This is Jesus' own direct statement, making the typology explicit rather than merely inferred.

options.text: He uses it only as an illustration of Israel's past disobedience with no reference to Himself.
options.note: Jesus applies the image directly to His own crucifixion, not merely as a historical illustration.

options.text: He rejects the story as an unreliable legend.
options.note: Jesus treats the account as real history and draws a direct parallel to His own mission.

options.text: The Gospels never reference this passage.
options.note: John 3:14-15 references it explicitly.

quiz.q: What happened when Israel asked Sihon king of the Amorites for peaceful passage through his land?

options.text: Sihon refused, gathered his army, and attacked Israel, but Israel defeated him and took his land.
options.note: Verses 21 to 25 describe this refusal, battle, and outcome.

options.text: Sihon granted passage immediately without conflict.
options.note: The opposite happened; Sihon refused and attacked, leading to his defeat.

options.text: Israel bypassed Sihon's territory entirely without contact.
options.note: The text describes direct negotiation, refusal, and battle with Sihon, not avoidance.

options.text: The outcome of this encounter is not recorded.
options.note: Verses 24 to 25 record Israel's victory and possession of the land in detail.

quiz.q: What later happened to the bronze serpent itself, according to 2 Kings 18:4?

options.text: King Hezekiah destroyed it because Israel had begun worshiping it as an idol.
options.note: 2 Kings 18:4 records Hezekiah's reform, breaking the bronze serpent, called Nehushtan, because it had become an object of worship.

options.text: It was placed permanently in the Most Holy Place as a treasured relic.
options.note: It was kept for a time but was ultimately destroyed once it became an idol, not enshrined as an ongoing object of reverence.

options.text: It was lost during Israel's conquest of Canaan.
options.note: It survived for centuries into the divided kingdom period, until Hezekiah's reform.

options.text: No later reference to it exists in Scripture.
options.note: 2 Kings 18:4 explicitly references it centuries later.

questions: Israel's impatience led them to despise the very provision God had given them daily. Where has restlessness tempted you to despise what God has already provided rather than trust Him for what is still ahead?
The people did not have to perform a cure, only look in faith at what God provided. Where are you still trying to earn healing or forgiveness instead of simply looking to Christ?

Jesus applied this very scene to His own crucifixion, being lifted up so that all who believe might live. How does knowing Jesus chose this image Himself deepen your confidence in what the cross accomplishes?
Centuries later, Israel turned this good gift into an idol, and it had to be destroyed. What good gifts in your own life are you tempted to worship instead of the God who gave them?
God judged real sin yet provided healing before the people even finished repenting. Where do you need to trust that God's grace can meet you as quickly as His judgment does?

translationNotes.note: Venomous snakes translates nachash saraph, literally fiery serpents, describing the burning pain of their venom rather than a literal fire; the same root later names the seraphim in Isaiah 6.
Bronze snake renders nechoshet, the same consonants as the Hebrew word for bronze, and the object is later called Nehushtan in 2 Kings 18:4, a name that plays on both bronze and serpent.

The Book of the Wars of the LORD, quoted in verses 14 to 15, is an otherwise unknown ancient source; its citation shows the biblical author drawing on existing records of Israel's early history rather than inventing the account.
